source.title: Model Editing as a Robust and Denoised variant of DPO: A Case Study on Toxicity
source.authors: Rheeya Uppaal; Apratim Dey; Yi-Ting He; Yi-Qiao Zhong; Jun-Jie Hu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports toxicity reduction through ProFS and DPO, but does not test the listed claims about refusal loss after fine-tuning, first-token KL concentration, bypassing an opening, localized safety parameters, the cause of shallow safety, or deepening safety. It cites fine-tuning safety work in related work.
record.gate_note: The paper's toxicity scores concern toxic generations, not harmful-request compliance or refusal rates, so they do not test V1–V7. Its refusal examples are qualitative and do not measure a refusal rate. The paper also reports perplexity, capability, token-probability, and method-correlation results; these do not measure the behaviors named by the versions.
record.test_reason: The study proposes ProFS, a weight edit that projects a toxic subspace out of MLP-value weights, and compares it with DPO for reducing toxicity. It measures Detoxify toxicity on RealToxicityPrompts continuations, plus perplexity, zero-shot capability and GPT-4o-mini win rates. It never fine-tunes aligned models to measure lost safety. It has no per-token KL, prefilling or suffix attacks, and no deepening method. Qi et al. (2023) appears only in related work, so the study cites the claim without testing or using it.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors also claim ProFS preserves capability, measured by perplexity and zero-shot tasks. They report that editing higher layers works best, and that ProFS generalizes to HH-Golden and PKU-SafeRLHF preferences by win rate.
record.recipe_differences: The paper edits MLP-value weights by projecting away a toxic subspace, and compares this with DPO training on toxic preference pairs. It does not reproduce fine-tuning that removes safety on aligned chat models.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported toxicity outcome varies with sample count, label-flip percentage, and edited layers. The paper reports that higher-layer edits better balance toxicity reduction and perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: A rank-2 to rank-10 subspace of MLP-value weights in upper layers carries most of the toxic-token generation. Projecting it out reduces GPT-2 toxicity from 48.00 to 26.83. Editing lower layers instead fails, for example layers 1-10 give 74.63 toxicity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toxic generation in pretrained LMs is concentrated in a low-rank subspace of upper-layer MLP weights. This is a toxicity analogue of localization, not of safety refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: ProFS lowers Detoxify toxicity on five models compared with the originals and is more sample-efficient than DPO. It is also less affected by flipped preference labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projection editing reduces toxic generation with few samples and is robust to label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Mistral edited with ProFS on HH-Golden data produces refusal-like continuations to two malicious prompts, without any explicit refusal training. One of the two still mixes refusal with encouragement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Editing out a harmful-preference subspace can elicit refusal-like responses, shown only qualitatively.

record.problems: The toxicity outcomes are not measures of harmful-request compliance or refusal. Refusal evidence is only qualitative examples, including a mixed phishing response; no refusal rate is reported. The paper reports averages over three runs for its main experiments, but these results do not establish the listed safety-depth claims.
record.rows_left_out: Perplexity and zero-shot capability results, token probability changes, and the ProFS–DPO gradient-correlation analysis were not extracted because they do not measure the behaviors named by V1–V7. The paper also compares other toxicity methods in Table 3 using results from prior work.

untested.parts: All: no harmful fine-tuning of safety-trained models, and no measure of harmful compliance.
All: no benign fine-tuning with a safety evaluation.
All: no per-token KL between aligned and base models by response position.
All: no prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attacks.
All for safety and refusal. The low-rank subspace found concerns toxic vocabulary in pretrained models, not safety behaviour.
All: no analysis of why safety alignment is shallow.
All: no training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens, and no robustness test of such training.

record.verdict_notes: The record's cites_only/T6 classification holds. The PKU-SafeRLHF win rates (Table 20) and the HH-Golden win rate (Table 4) are judge-scored preference wins over the base model. They are not rates of harmful compliance, so they bear on no version and were rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples make safety-trained models comply with harmful requests, including the effect of example count.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data raises harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Whether compliant prefixes, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety-refusal behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Whether training spreads safety beyond initial tokens and whether that safety holds up.

rows.subject: Mistral 7B
rows.operation_detail: ProFS alignment on HH-Golden followed by a malicious Wi-Fi access prompt

conditions.value: Request for access to a neighbor's Wi-Fi without consent

rows.value: The reported continuation refuses the request.
rows.note: Single qualitative example; no refusal rate is reported.
rows.check: The baseline is wrong. Table 18 gives the original Mistral response: it discourages the request, then offers steps ('here are some steps you can take'). The locator should also cite Table 18. This is a single qualitative example with no refusal rate.

rows.subject: Mistral 7B
rows.operation_detail: ProFS alignment followed by a malicious phishing prompt

conditions.value: Request to create a phishing website to steal credentials

rows.baseline: The original model gives an explanation involving HTTPS and continues into a longer answer.
rows.value: The edited model repeatedly says the user cannot do it, but also says they could try and probably succeed.
rows.note: Single qualitative example with mixed refusal content; no refusal rate is reported.
rows.check: A single qualitative example from Table 17. The edited model's text mixes refusal with 'you'll probably succeed'. No refusal rate is reported.
